newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: YEAREND - S.AFRICA IN 1997: IT'S THE ECONOMY, STUPID.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND - S.AFRICA IN 1997: IT'S THE ECONOMY, STUPID.

text.p: South Africa probed the truth about its ugly past, quelled a Zulu feud, endured a crime wave and smashed some diplomatic china this year. But these were ripples in a current of destiny driven by the economy.

President Nelson Mandela made triumphant tours abroad, fell in love with Graca Machel, saw his grim Robben Island prison turning into a museum and signed into law a brand new constitution cementing democracy and enshrining human rights.

"Those who sought their own freedom in the domination of others were doomed to ignominious failure," Mandela said after signing the constitution on December 10 at the site of the 1960 Sharpeville massacre.
"Out of such experience was born the understanding that there could be no lasting peace, no security, no prosperity in this land unless all enjoyed freedom and justice as equals."
Spiritually, the nation seems past the worst. Its exuberance shines in sporting prowess and parliamentary vigour.
But its problems glare in dirt-poor shantytowns, idle manpower and downtown streets abandoned at night to crime.
As Finance Minister Trevor Manuel quickly learned, creating wealth and the even trickier art of keeping it have become the crucial yardstick of success. But there lies the dilemma:

"Growth which does not feed the poor will collapse... redistribution without expanded production cannot be sustained, prosperity without security of life and property holds no appeal," Manuel said last month.
Academics may debate whether economic growth is a sufficient index of human development, but for South Africa that would be a dangerous luxury.
PENT-UP BLACK ASPIRATIONS

In 1997, economic forces will continue to propel this island of relative prosperity at the end of the world's poorest continent, struggling to steer a course between pent-up black aspirations and the rocky limitations of sustainable growth.

"The most critical phase lies ahead," said Standard Bank chairman Conrad Strauss, citing "the potential conflict between economic imperatives and social and political demands" and uttering what has become a truism.

Put plainly, Mandela's government cannot afford everything at once, no matter how loud, just and even angry the demands for jobs, housing, clean water, better schools and basic services. To survive and prosper, the economy must grow strongly.

At some point in 1996, South Africa's peaceful transition from white supremacy to majority rule became yesterday's miracle. The glow faded, as Mandela told everyone it would, and the cliffs of a new challenge loomed above the infant democracy.
Its currency, the rand, has plunged relentlessly since January, losing 30 percent of its value against the dollar.

Foreign investors, no longer misty-eyed over Mandela's saintly forbearance towards white rulers who shut him away for 27 years, saw red warning-lights: runaway crime, stalled privatisation plans, inefficient industry, Marxist-led unions.

Educated whites continued to trickle out of the country, betting that without a Mandela, now 78 years old and "coming nearer to sleeping for eternity" in his own words, South Africa would slip and slide into some familiar African tragedy.
In March, Finance Minister Chris Liebenberg resigned, handing over to Manuel, who got off to a rocky start with sceptical markets.

But backed by Mandela and his likely successor Thabo Mbeki, Manuel has stayed the course, coaxing from the ruling African National Congress (ANC) a blueprint for economic growth that embraces free market capitalism.
Mbeki globe-trotted tirelessly to reassure investors that fears of profligate statism were unfounded.
DEMOCRACY COMES OF AGE
In May, ex-President F.W. de Klerk, declaring the new republic had come of age, pulled his National Party out of coalition government to provide an invigorating opposition.
A National Party victory in Cape province council elections demonstrated democracy at work two years after Mandela won a historic landslide in South Africa's first free ballot.

In Kwazulu-Natal province, where internecine Zulu feuding had twice stalled elections, Mandela showed toughness, deploying 30,000 armed men to quell the blood-letting so that voting could finally take place in June.
Nobel peace laureate Desmond Tutu, the Anglican archbishop, redoubled his efforts to heal the wounds inflicted by 40 years of apartheid and the guerrilla war to topple white supremacy.
Chairing a roving truth commission, he persuaded undercover apparatchiks of the former regime to publicly confess crimes of torture and killing, in return for a chance of amnesty.
Whereas de Klerk had apologised for apartheid, his hardline predecessor P.W. Botha broke his long silence only to announce he had nothing to beg forgiveness for.
PRIVATISATION, FOR MANDELA TOO

In foreign affairs, Mandela's inexperienced and idealistic team tripped over Cuba, Libya and Iran -- countries that helped the ANC in its outlaw days but were now placed beyond the pale by powerful Western governments.
Mandela dithered over using his clout to defend human rights in Nigeria or intervene in the unravelling Great Lakes crisis.
Reluctant to bite the bullet, he announced last month his government was dumping ties with Taiwan in favour of Beijing -- but would delay final severance with the rival China for a year.
Clumsy or not, it demonstrated diplomatic realism to match maturing economic realism.
South Africa's biggest corporation, Anglo American , also did its bit for the "rainbow nation" in 1996, selling control of two healthy chunks of its empire to black interests.
But investors were scathing about slow privatisation "which lacks a driver, clear objectives, financial estimates and, crucially, a time element", said Standard Bank's Strauss.
Progress on privatisation is viewed as the litmus test for South Africa's commitment to economic reform in 1997, which some economic analysts believe could be a make-or-break year.
A different privatisation beckons for Mandela.

In 12 months from now, growing weary and looking forward to his twilight years in the company of the widow of Mozambique liberation leader Samora Machel, he plans to resign as leader of the ANC, his first step towards quitting public life when elections come around in April 1999.
Until then, Mandela's long walk to freedom continues.
